clinicalPearls: An incidental ultrasound finding of multiple tiny, usually sub-millimetre to a few millimetres, non-shadowing echogenic foci scattered through the testicular parenchyma
Classically described as a 'starry sky' appearance, with classic or diffuse microlithiasis defined as five or more microliths per ultrasound field
Usually asymptomatic and discovered during scrotal imaging performed for another reason such as pain, subfertility, or a lump
The association with testicular germ-cell tumour is real, but its clinical significance and the need for surveillance are debated, since most men with microlithiasis never develop cancer

Risk is considered higher when microlithiasis coexists with other factors - subfertility, testicular atrophy, cryptorchidism or prior undescended testis, a personal or family history of germ-cell tumour, or a contralateral tumour
In the absence of additional risk factors most guidance advises teaching testicular self-examination rather than routine repeat ultrasound, reserving surveillance imaging for higher-risk men
Microlithiasis is not itself a premalignant lesion and needs no treatment; the emphasis is on appropriate risk stratification
reference.pathophysiology: Testicular microlithiasis represents calcified concretions within the lumen of the seminiferous tubules. Cells that degenerate within a tubule fail to be cleared and act as a nidus for laminated calcium deposition surrounded by a glycoprotein matrix, producing the characteristic tiny echogenic foci seen on ultrasound. The same disordered tubular environment that favours these calcifications is thought to be shared with abnormalities of the germinal epithelium, which may explain the statistical association with germ-cell neoplasia and with subfertility, even though the microliths themselves are not a precursor lesion.
additionalInvestigations: Scrotal ultrasound to characterise and quantify the foci and assess for any associated mass
Testicular tumour markers (AFP, beta-hCG, LDH) if a discrete lesion is seen
Clinical examination with teaching of testicular self-examination
Interval ultrasound surveillance in higher-risk patients
redFlags: A discrete focal testicular mass on ultrasound
A rapidly changing testicular size or a new hard lump
Coexisting cryptorchidism or a prior germ-cell tumour
reference.prognosis: In isolation the prognosis is excellent and the great majority of men remain free of malignancy; the outlook is chiefly determined by the presence or absence of additional germ-cell-tumour risk factors.
pitfalls: Over-investigating low-risk men with repeated ultrasounds and provoking unnecessary anxiety
Conversely, failing to arrange surveillance in men who have microlithiasis together with significant risk factors
Assuming microlithiasis is itself premalignant and requires treatment
Not teaching and documenting testicular self-examination as the key safety-net
references: European Society of Urogenital Radiology guidance on testicular microlithiasis
management: Risk-stratify each patient by the presence of additional germ-cell-tumour risk factors such as subfertility, testicular atrophy, cryptorchidism or a personal or family history of germ-cell tumour
Teach regular testicular self-examination as the principal strategy for men with isolated microlithiasis and no additional risk factors
Reserve interval scrotal ultrasound surveillance for higher-risk men rather than applying it routinely
Investigate any discrete mass promptly with tumour markers AFP, beta-hCG and LDH and urological assessment to exclude germ-cell tumour
Offer semen analysis to subfertile men, given the association with impaired spermatogenesis
Reassure low-risk men that the great majority never develop malignancy
Refer to urology when additional risk factors or a suspicious lesion are present
